---
title: "Is Inflation Back?"
subtitle: "Prices are rising faster again, mostly because of gas. And for the first time in years, paychecks are falling behind."
author: "SixtyEight95"
date: "2026-11-19"
categories: [inflation, cost of living, wages, energy]
image: infographic.png
---

```{r setup}
source("../../R/fred.R")
source("../../R/inflation_data.R")
library(plotly)
library(knitr)
pct  <- function(x) paste0(formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1), "%")
pct2 <- function(x) paste0(formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2), "%")
```

After the 2021–2023 price surge finally cooled, a lot of people hoped inflation was behind us. This year, it
started climbing again. We looked at the government's own numbers to see how big the rebound is, what's
driving it, and what it means for your paycheck.

## The short answer

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Prices are up **`r pct(infl_now$all)`** from a year ago (`r month_label(infl_now$date)`), up from **`r pct(infl_low$all)`** in
`r month_label(infl_low$date)`. Most of the jump is **energy**: gasoline is up **`r pct(infl_now$gasoline)`**. Without food and energy,
inflation is a calmer **`r pct(infl_now$core)`**.

But it's enough to bite: pay is up only **`r pct(infl_now$pay)`**, so the average paycheck now buys **less** than it did a
year ago for the first time since early 2023.
:::

## The rebound

```{r rebound chart}
#| fig-height: 4.5
recent <- inflation %>% filter(date >= as.Date("2019-01-01")) %>%
  select(date, `All prices` = all, `Without food & energy (core)` = core) %>%
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "series", values_to = "rate")

p <- ggplot(recent, aes(date, rate, color = series, group = series,
                        text = paste0(series, ", ", format(date, "%b %Y"), ": ", pct(rate)))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 2, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(iran_strike), linetype = "dotted", color = "#D69E2E") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("All prices" = "#C53030", "Without food & energy (core)" = "#2A9D8F")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Change from a year earlier (%)", color = NULL)
ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") %>% layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = 1.08)) %>% config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

The dashed line is the Federal Reserve's 2% target. The dotted line marks the U.S. and Israeli strike on Iran in
late February 2026, which disrupted oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Notice that the red line (all prices)
jumped right after, while the teal line (everything except food and energy) barely moved. That tells you this
rebound is mostly about energy, not a broad-based surge like 2022.

## What's driving it

```{r drivers table}
tribble(
  ~Category, ~`Change from a year ago`,
  "Gasoline", pct(infl_now$gasoline),
  "All energy (gas, electricity, heating)", pct(infl_now$energy),
  "Housing costs (shelter)", pct(infl_now$shelter),
  "Food", pct(infl_now$food),
  "Everything except food & energy", pct(infl_now$core),
  "All prices", pct(infl_now$all),
  "Wholesale prices (producer prices)", pct(infl_now$wholesale)
) %>% kable(align = "lr", caption = paste("Consumer and producer price indexes,", month_label(infl_now$date), "vs. a year earlier. Source: BLS via FRED."))
```

Two things to watch:

- **Wholesale prices are up `r pct(infl_now$wholesale)`.** Producer prices measure what businesses pay. When those rise
  faster than consumer prices, some of it tends to show up on store shelves later.
- **Food is starting to climb.** Food prices rose `r pct(infl_now$food)` over the year, and higher fuel and shipping costs
  can push grocery prices up with a delay.

## What it means for your paycheck

```{r real pay chart}
#| fig-height: 4
rp <- real_pay %>% filter(date >= as.Date("2019-01-01"), !is.na(real_pay_change))
p2 <- ggplot(rp, aes(date, real_pay_change, group = 1,
             text = paste0(format(date, "%b %Y"), ": real pay ", ifelse(real_pay_change >= 0, "up ", "down "),
                           pct(abs(real_pay_change)), " vs a year earlier"))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey40") +
  geom_line(color = "#1F4E5A", linewidth = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Pay growth minus price growth (%)")
ggplotly(p2, tooltip = "text") %>% config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

This line shows whether paychecks are beating prices. Above zero, the average worker's pay is growing faster than
prices; below zero, it's falling behind. From mid-2023 through 2025, pay comfortably outran prices. In
`r month_label(real_now$date)`, it dipped below zero: **`r pct(real_now$real_pay_change)`**.

## The Fed is raising rates again

To fight inflation, the Federal Reserve raises interest rates, which makes borrowing more expensive and cools
spending. After holding rates steady for most of 2026, the Fed has started nudging them up: the federal funds rate
rose from **`r pct2(fed_low$rate)`** to **`r pct2(fed_now$rate)`** this fall, and many forecasters expect another increase in December.
For households, that means **higher rates on credit cards, car loans, and mortgages.**

## The fine print

- **Inflation numbers are averages.** If you drive a lot, energy inflation hits you much harder than someone who
  works from home.
- **"Core" inflation** leaves out food and energy because they swing wildly; it's a better guide to the long-term
  trend, but you still pay for gas and groceries.
- **Pay is the average hourly earnings** of production and nonsupervisory workers, before taxes.
- **This can change quickly.** If oil prices fall (as they did briefly this month on hopes of calmer fighting with
  Iran), headline inflation could ease fast.

## The bottom line

Inflation is back, but it's a different animal than 2022: so far it's mostly an energy shock, with everything else
rising at a more normal pace. That's the good news. The bad news is that it's enough to put paychecks behind prices
again, and the Fed's response means borrowing is getting more expensive too.

---

**How we did this.** All figures are from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the Federal Reserve via
[FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/): CPI for all urban consumers (CPIAUCSL), CPI less food and energy (CPILFESL),
energy (CPIENGSL), food (CPIUFDSL), shelter (CUSR0000SAH1), gasoline (CUSR0000SETB01), producer prices for final
demand (PPIFIS), average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory employees (AHETPI), and the effective
federal funds rate (FEDFUNDS). Changes are compared with the same month a year earlier.
